  > 
  > **1 (M3).** Done: `REPRO_NOTES.md` has no role name and no "reserved by the objective" wording (the exposure disclosure is kept, now worded as "a published paper on this task, not consulted, not cited"); README line about the pipeline reworded; no docstring names a repository or role (grep for experiment-repo, paper-repo, figtab, story/idea/venue, ht-resource, hutian, ResearchWorld, "analysis role", objective, reserved: no match in the package).
  > 
  > **2 (M2).** `09_paired.py` is called by `run_all.sh`'s analyze stage and writes `results/inner50/paired_vs_main.csv`; the rebuild prints the paired column from it.
  > 
  > **4 (m1), both tested from existing files; scripts `10_ceiling_centred.py`, `11_extrap_bias.py`, outputs `results/ceiling_centred.csv`, `results/extrap_bias.csv`.**
  > - *Centred vs uncentred Brier — does not explain the interpolation gap.* IRT predictor (right panel), uniform design, n=100, geometric mean over non-thin benchmarks. Reference √(1−q) uncentred / centred (Brier minus the squared mean residual on the unsampled items, per target and draw) / observed: interp 0.806 / 0.802 / 0.700; lineage 0.819 / 0.815 / 0.727; extrap 0.847 / 0.823 / 0.854; extrap50 0.900 / 0.861 / 0.975; extrap10 0.815 / 0.800 / 0.820 (n benchmarks 13 / 12 / 13 / 13 / 7). Centring moves interpolation by 0.004 of a 0.106 gap, so the sentence "may explain part of the interpolation gap" should be replaced by "centring the Brier score changes the reference by 0.004 (interpolation) and 0.024 (extrapolation); the gap in interpolation is not explained by it". The uncentred columns reproduce the paper's 0.81/0.82/0.85 and 0.70/0.73/0.85.
  > - *Why ridge extrapolates better — only on one design, and only partly.* Extrapolation, n=100, 13 non-thin benchmarks, 799 targets: signed bias of the model-based estimators regressed on the target's distance above the lowest target (both in sd of the benchmark's target scores). Slope (bias per sd of gap) / bias of the top quarter of targets (sd units) / share of squared bias in MSE: balanced design — IRT model −0.61 / −2.69 / 0.96; kNN −0.88 / −3.20 / 0.99; ridge −0.27 / −0.99 / 0.60. Uniform design — IRT −0.60 / −2.68 / 0.95; kNN −0.89 / −3.23 / 0.99; ridge −0.54 / −1.92 / 0.85 (strat is the same as uniform). So ridge's bias grows about half as fast as the logistic predictors' on the balanced design, and about as fast on uniform/strat; the advantage is a property of ridge × balanced, not of ridge alone. I did not test why (the design balances the item features the ridge uses, but that is a reading, not a result). Suggested sentence: "ridge on a balanced design has about half the extrapolation bias slope of the logistic predictors (−0.27 vs −0.61/−0.88 per target-sd above the sources); on uniform or stratified designs it does not (−0.54)."
  > 
  > **3 (M6), feasible, running now.** I cloned the independent public repositories (tinyBenchmarks tutorials + the py-irt fork they require; Anchor Points) and wrote `scripts/12_public_baselines.py`, which runs their recipes on our matrices with our folds, targets and 10 selection seeds, n=100, interp and extrap, the seven OLL benchmarks:
  > - stage A (all folds): tinyBenchmarks anchors by KMeans on correctness with cluster-mass weights; Anchor Points Weighted (k-medoids on 1−corr, cluster-size weights, public `kmedoids` package);
  > - stage B (py-irt fork, multidim 2PL D=10, 2000 epochs, as in their tutorial; interpolation fold 0 and extrapolation; MMLU-Pro excluded for cost): tinyBenchmarks IRT-embedding anchors and p-IRT with their `estimate_ability_parameters`. gp-IRT (needs their validation-fit λ) and the Anchor Points predictor (needs class probabilities) are not run.
  > Results go next to our `anchor|mean`, `anchor|irt-plugin` on the same targets/folds as ratio to uniform×mean; jobs are queued on a loaded host, so expect them in later turns. The code of the other authors is not copied into our reposit
